text: Pain relievers are in almost every home, and we reach for them at every fever. It feels like the fastest way to help.
Call or visit your health center before giving any medicine for a fever that might be dengue.
WHO fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue (2025): avoid anti-inflammatory pain relievers because of bleeding risk
Dengue is only a problem during the rainy season.
Dengue can spread all year. Cases peak in the rainy months, so empty water containers every week.
Dengue news comes mostly with the rains, so the dry months feel safe. Good habits are easy to drop when the danger seems gone.
Search your home for standing water every week, all year. Ask your barangay health worker about dengue nearby.
WHO fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue (2025); DOH statements on year-round dengue (2025)
Leftover antibiotics can be shared with a sick family member.
Antibiotics are chosen for one person and one infection. Sharing them can harm and fuel resistance.
Sharing medicine feels like caring, and it saves money. If it helped one person, it seems sure to help another.
Do not share or save antibiotics. Ask a pharmacist how to throw away leftovers safely.
WHO fact sheet: Antimicrobial resistance (2026); CDC Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts
Generic medicines are weaker than branded ones.
Registered generics have the same active ingredient as the brand and must meet quality standards.
We often think a higher price means better quality. A familiar name on the box feels more trustworthy than a plain label.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist about a registered generic. You can check registration on the FDA Philippines portal.
Generics Act of 1988 (RA 6675); US FDA: Generic Drug Facts; FDA Philippines verification portal
Medicine from any online seller is the same as from a pharmacy.
Fake and substandard medicines are often sold online. Buy from licensed pharmacies.
Online shops are cheap and close at hand, and the boxes look just like the real ones. For many families, the pharmacy is far.
Check the product on the FDA Philippines portal and buy from a licensed pharmacy. Ask your pharmacist when unsure.
WHO fact sheet: Substandard and falsified medical products (2024)
The more vitamins you take, the healthier you get.
Too much of some vitamins and minerals can harm you. Supplements do not replace a varied diet.
Vitamins sound like pure goodness, and ads promise energy and strong immunity. More of a good thing feels even better.
Show your health worker every vitamin and supplement you take, and ask whether you really need it.
NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Dietary Supplements, What You Need to Know (consumer fact sheet)
Vaccines cause autism.
Many large studies, reviewed again by WHO safety experts in 2025, show vaccines do not cause autism.
Signs of autism often show up around the age children get vaccines, so the timing feels connected. Parents want answers, and that worry comes from love.
Bring your worries to your health worker. Check WHO or DOH vaccine safety pages, not forwarded posts.
WHO GACVS statement on vaccines and autism (December 2025)
Catching measles naturally is better than getting the vaccine.
Measles can cause pneumonia, blindness, brain swelling and death. The vaccine protects without those risks.
"Natural" sounds gentle and strong, and many older relatives had measles as kids and got through it. Those memories feel like proof.
Ask your barangay health center about measles vaccines for your child. They are free.
WHO fact sheet: Measles (2026); DOH national immunization program
Too many vaccines at once will overload a baby.
Babies meet many germs every day. Vaccines given together are tested and do not overload the immune system.
Watching a small baby get several shots in one visit is hard for any parent. Wanting to protect them is natural.
Ask your health worker why the vaccines are given together and what to expect after the visit.
Gavi VaccinesWork: Do multiple vaccines overload a child's immune system? (2025)
Vaccines are only for babies and children.
Some vaccines, like flu and pneumonia vaccines, are also advised for seniors and some adults.
Most vaccine talk is about babies, and many adults have not had a shot since school. It is easy to think we are done.
Ask your barangay health center which vaccines are advised for you, especially if you are 60 or older.
WHO position paper: Vaccines against influenza (2022); Expanded Senior Citizens Act (RA 9994)
Cervical cancer cannot be prevented.
Most cervical cancer can be prevented with HPV vaccination and regular screening.
Cancer can feel like bad luck that nobody controls. Fear makes many of us avoid check-ups, even the ones that could help.
Ask your health center about the HPV vaccine for girls and cervical screening for women.
WHO fact sheet: Cervical cancer (2026)
A biopsy or an operation makes cancer spread.
The chance that surgery spreads cancer is extremely low. Delaying care gives cancer time to grow.
Someone we knew may have gotten worse after an operation, and the story stuck. The cancer was often already advanced, but the operation got the blame.
Share your worries with your doctor before deciding. Bring a family member to help you ask questions.
US National Cancer Institute: Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions (2024)
Only people who eat a lot of sweets get diabetes.
Type 2 diabetes is linked to weight, little exercise and family history, not just sweets.
Diabetes is often just called "sugar", so it makes sense to blame sweets. People who skip dessert may feel safe.
Ask your barangay health center for a blood sugar check, especially if diabetes runs in your family.
WHO fact sheet: Diabetes (2024)
Maintenance medicines will ruin your kidneys.
Uncontrolled high blood pressure and sugar harm the kidneys. Ask your doctor before changing any medicine.
Taking pills every day for years is worrying, and many families know someone on dialysis. Fearing the medicine is understandable.
Bring your kidney worries to your doctor. Ask about check-ups that watch your kidneys while you take medicine.
WHO fact sheets: Hypertension (2025) and Diabetes (2024)
Pricking the fingertips can save someone having a stroke.
A stroke is an emergency. Get the person to a hospital right away; pricking fingers only wastes time.
In a scary moment, a simple trick feels like something we can do with our own hands. The tip is often shared as a life-saver.
Learn the signs: face drooping, arm weakness, speech trouble. If you see them, go to the hospital at once.
CONTENT_GUIDE red flags (stroke signs); American Stroke Association F.A.S.T. warning signs; Full Fact check on pin-prick stroke claims
Depression is just a weak mind. Be strong and it will pass.
Depression is a common health condition, not weakness. It can be treated, and help is available.
Many of us were raised to endure hardship quietly. Saying "be strong" is how families try to lift each other up.
Talk to a health worker or someone you trust. For thoughts of self-harm, call the crisis hotline 1553 now.
WHO fact sheet: Depressive disorder (2026); NCMH crisis hotline 1553
Children only need deworming if you can see worms.
Worm infections often show no signs. Free deworming at school and health centers protects children.
If a child looks healthy and eats well, there seems to be nothing to treat. Worms are not something families like to talk about.
Ask your barangay health center or school about the free deworming schedule for your child.
WHO fact sheet: Soil-transmitted helminth infections (2023); DOH school deworming program
Formula milk makes babies smarter than breast milk.
Breast milk is the best first food and protects babies from infections. Health workers can help.
Formula ads show bright, strong babies, and many moms worry their milk is not enough. Wanting the best for a baby is love.
Ask your health center or a breastfeeding counselor for help, especially if breastfeeding feels hard.
WHO fact sheet: Infant and young child feeding (2026)
Only the elderly can get heat stroke.
Anyone can get heat stroke, including young workers and athletes. It is a medical emergency.
Heat warnings usually mention lolos and lolas. Young people feel strong and used to the sun.
Drink water, rest in the shade and check on others. Get help fast if someone becomes confused or faints.
WHO fact sheet: Climate change, heat and health (2026)
TB runs in the family, so it is passed down by blood.
TB spreads through the air when a sick person coughs. It is preventable and curable, with free treatment.
TB often shows up in several people in one home, so it looks inherited. Living close together is the real reason.
If someone at home has TB, ask the health center to check the rest of the household.
WHO fact sheet: Tuberculosis (2026); DOH TB program
A call in my child's voice asking for hospital money is real.
Voices can be cloned with AI. Hang up and call the person back on a number you know.
Hearing a loved one in trouble makes the heart race. Scammers count on that love and rush you before you can think.
Call back on a saved number or ask a family question only they would know. Report scams to hotline 1326.
US FTC consumer alert: Scammers use AI to enhance their family emergency schemes (2023); CICC hotline 1326
Hundreds of happy comments prove a product works.
Comments and reviews can be fake or paid. Many stories together are still not evidence.
When many people seem happy, it feels safe to join them. Stories from people like us feel more real than studies.
Check the product on the FDA Philippines portal and ask a health worker instead of trusting the comments.
US FTC Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (2024); CONTENT_GUIDE Kwento Kim trick
A product that cures many diseases at once is a breakthrough.
Claiming to cure many unrelated diseases is a classic warning sign, not a breakthrough.
Living with several illnesses is tiring and costly. One product for everything sounds like the answer to a prayer.
Check the product on the FDA Philippines portal, and look for "No approved therapeutic claims" on the label.
US FDA: Health Fraud Scams ("one product does it all" red flag); CONTENT_GUIDE Miracle Mike signs
What I tell a health chatbot stays private, like a clinic visit.
Chats may be stored or used to improve the AI. Keep your full name, ID numbers and diagnoses out.
Chatbots feel personal and patient, so it is easy to open up. Unlike a clinic, the privacy rules for chats are often unclear.
Read the app's privacy settings before sharing. Bring personal health questions to your health worker instead.
NPC Advisory No. 2024-04: Guidelines on AI and the Data Privacy Act (2024); CONTENT_GUIDE AI facts
If many people post about fever online, it is an official outbreak.
Online posts are early clues. Health workers check them first, and health authorities announce real outbreaks.
When the feed fills with sick neighbours, it feels like proof. Worry for our families makes every post seem urgent.
Look for an announcement from DOH or your city health office. Ask your barangay health worker what they know.
WHO Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS): online signals are verified by analysts before they count as events
An outbreak warning in the group chat is always true.
Rumours often spread faster than checks. Real outbreak news comes from DOH and local health offices.
Family chats are where we look out for each other. A warning from someone we love feels too important to doubt.
Before forwarding, check DOH or city health office pages. If you cannot confirm it, do not share it yet.
WHO: WHO public health research agenda for managing infodemics (2021)
The flu is just a bad cold.
Flu often starts suddenly with fever and body aches. It can be serious for seniors, young children and pregnant women.
Both start with a cough and a runny nose, and most people get better at home. So it is easy to treat them the same.
Ask your health center about the yearly flu vaccine. Get help fast for trouble breathing or chest pain.
WHO fact sheet: Influenza (seasonal) (2025)
The flu vaccine gives you the flu.
Flu shots cannot cause flu. A sore arm or mild fever may happen and passes quickly.
Some people catch a cold soon after a shot, so the shot gets the blame. Protection also takes about two weeks to build.
Ask your health worker what to expect after a flu shot and when the protection starts.
CDC: Flu Vaccine Safety Information (2024); WHO fact sheet: Influenza (seasonal) (2025)
A small cough is no reason to cover my mouth or wear a mask.
Even a mild cough can spread germs. Cover it with a tissue or your elbow, and wear a mask around others.
When we feel only a little sick, we do not want to make a fuss. Masks can also feel awkward in a crowd.
Cough into your elbow, wash your hands and stay home when sick if you can. Mask up around seniors and babies.
WHO fact sheet: Influenza (seasonal) (2025): cover coughs and sneezes, clean hands, stay home when unwell
Pneumonia is just a bad cold that goes away on its own.
Pneumonia is a lung infection that can be serious. Fast or hard breathing needs a health worker right away.
Pneumonia often starts like a cough or cold, so it is easy to wait it out. Many families hope rest at home is enough.
Watch how a sick child or senior breathes. Go to the health center now if breathing is fast or hard.
WHO fact sheet: Pneumonia in children (2022): danger signs; vaccines and clean air prevent many cases
A quick rinse with water is enough to clean my hands.
Washing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds removes far more germs and helps stop infections spreading.
